title: Noise-limited secret key agreement with twin optical physically unclonable functions
abstract: We investigate the use of twin optical fingerprints derived from correlated physical unclonable functions (PUFs), as a hardware-based platform for cryptographic key generation and distribution. Each fingerprint is associated with a random, yet reproducible speckle pattern, generated when coherent light is scattered by a disordered optical structure. We consider a pair of correlated optical PUFs, and study the conditions under which two honest parties can establish a common secret key, despite fabrication-induced variability and environmental noise. An explicit information-theoretic key-agreement protocol is developed, incorporating secure sketches, error reconciliation, and privacy amplification. We quantify information leakage due to public helper data, and derive lower bounds on the length of the final secret key. The analysis identifies the noise regimes in which secure key agreement is feasible, and examines the performance of both practical and near-capacity reconciliation schemes. Finally, we discuss how twin optical PUFs could be integrated into quantum key distribution (QKD) networks, as a mechanism for establishing an initial pre-shared secret key between two honest users, without relying on computational assumptions or trusted third parties.
summary: This work proposes using twin optical PUFs—which derive their randomness from correlated speckle patterns generated by light scattering—to establish a secret key. It develops a rigorous, information-theoretic protocol for key agreement that accounts for environmental noise and fabrication variability. This offers a hardware-based alternative to traditional quantum key distribution methods.
main_problem: The paper investigates establishing a shared secret key between two parties using twin optical Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs) as a hardware-based platform for cryptography.
main_result: An explicit information-theoretic protocol is developed that quantifies the achievable lower bound on the final secret key length, identifying noise regimes where secure agreement is feasible without relying on computational assumptions.
method: The core method involves developing an information-theoretic key-agreement protocol incorporating secure sketches, error reconciliation, and privacy amplification applied to correlated PUF responses.
model_or_system: The physical platform utilizes twin O-PUFs, where the fingerprint is a speckle pattern generated by coherent light scattering through disordered optical structures. The model mathematically describes the output electric field using linear scattering theory involving transmission matrices.
key_observables: Information leakage due to public helper data; lower bounds on the length of the final secret key; Bit Error Rate (BER) between raw keys.
important_parameters: Fabrication-induced variability ($\sigma_F$) and environmental noise ($\sigma_E$); the maximum allowed Hamming distance ($t$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes linear scattering theory in the diffusive limit, challenge uniformity, and that the adversary is limited to observing public classical communication.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates the main steps of key agreement using twin PUFs, detailing the flow from raw key generation through sketching, reconciliation, and amplification.
paper_structure: The paper first models the physical process using correlated O-PUFs. It then develops the information-theoretic protocol (sketching $ightarrow$ reconciliation $ightarrow$ amplification). Finally, it analyzes the security bounds based on noise regimes and discusses integration into QKD networks.
why_interesting: While not directly about quantum dynamics, the reliance on complex physical phenomena like light scattering in disordered media to generate high-entropy random numbers touches upon open questions at the intersection of condensed matter physics (disorder) and information theory.
